He helped write the Constitution. Then he helped change it. James Madison initially questioned the need for a bill of rights. Do you know what persuaded him to become its champion? This Constitution Day, explore how the courage to challenge and the humility to reconsider helped strengthen protections for individual liberty. Its a story about the civic virtues that make self-government work. Watch The Debate that Built the Bill of Rights, part of BRIs Constitution Day programming:  https://lnkd.in/e4KUbzTZ  #ConstitutionDay  #CivicEducation  #BillOfRights

25 years later, we remember not only what happened on September 11, 2001, but how people responded. First responders ran toward danger. Passengers fought back. In moments of extraordinary peril, people chose to protect others, offering enduring examples of courage and self-sacrifice. Their example calls each generation to consider what civic virtue requires of us. Civic education helps ensure that their sacrifice is not only remembered, but understood. Watch BRI's short video, then explore the Self-Sacrifice in a Firehouse on 9/11 lesson from American Portraits, which examines the story of 1 New York City firehouse that lost 12 men that day:  https://bit.ly/4gZxATr  #September11  #CivicEducation  #AmericanHistory

6 stops. 11 years. 1 road to the Constitution. How did the United States travel from declaring independence in 1776 to establishing a new Constitution in 1787? The second video in BRIs Constitution Day 2026 programming turns that essential story into an engaging road trip for young learners. Along the way, students discover how Americans worked to build a nation capable of protecting rights, establishing justice, and securing liberty. Climb into the Treehouse car and explore the road to "We the People." Watch Road Trip: From the Declaration to the Constitution:  https://bit.ly/42cJB0M  #ConstitutionDay  #CivicEducation  #AmericanHistory  #ElementaryEducation

The road to the Constitution begins with a printing press. Why did Mary Katharine Goddard risk placing her own name beneath the Declaration of Independence? How did Mercy Otis Warren bring revolutionary ideas into the homes of everyday Americans? In the first video from BRIs Constitution Day 2026 programming, discover how 2 women used ink, information, and courage to help citizens understand independence and prepare for the responsibilities of self-government. History looks inevitable only in hindsight. BRI Director of Communications Lindsay Moran shares how a living-room debate sparked by Young Washington became a lesson in historical perspective: understanding not only what people chose, but what they knew, believed, and risked when they made that choice. That kind of inquiry is at the heart of history and civics education. It asks students to examine evidence, question assumptions, and understand the past before deciding what they think about it. For more on how to inspire young thinkers using the film, check out BRI's resources exploring the life and times of George Washington:  https://lnkd.in/gzcH4kjd Big thanks to Daniels Fund for helping make these resources possible.  #YoungWashington  #HistoryEducation  #CivicsEducation

I was watching Young Washington (again!) with my boyfriend when he casually announced: "Yeah, if Id been alive then, I probably would have been on the side of the British.  Whaaaaaat? (He might as well have told me he cheated on ME.) How can you even SAY that?  I demanded. He calmly explained that if he had actually been a young man living in the colonies at the time it probably wouldnt have occurred to him that British rule was something to overthrow. The revolutionaries would have seemed like radicals. I was having none of it. "Nope. Not me. I would have been with the Americans!  Maybe not on the battlefield. But definitely in spirit. (Possibly as a spy. 🤔 ) But then, annoyingly, I started to realize he had a point. We love to - or at least I love to - imagine that if we had lived at some pivotal moment in history, we know exactly what we would have done. We would have recognized the right side immediately. We would have been brave. We would have questioned assumptions everyone else took for granted. But of course, we know how the story ends. The people living it didn't. Even George Washington spent his early adulthood fighting on Britain's side in the French and Indian War. He served alongside British forces and actually wanted a commission in the regular British Army but the higher-ups repeatedly said no. This man who would eventually command the entire Continental Army didn't start out knowing that was where history, or even his own convictions, would take him. That's what stayed with me after our "argument." History gets flattened when we look backward. Choices seem obvious because we already know which ideas prevailed and which causes succeeded. Living through history, as each of us does every day, is different. It's messy and uncertain. People make decisions based on incomplete information (nowadays sometimes mis- or disinformation), personal interests, assumptions and biases, greed, fear, courage, whatever . . . not to mention NO idea what the next chapter is going to say. One thing I love about my job at BRI is that I'm encountering questions like this every day. Not simply, What happened? but Why did people make the choices they made? What did the world look like from where they were standing? And what might we have done if we'd been standing there too? Those questions make history a lot more interesting to me, and a little more humbling. (Still . . . pretty sure I would have been a Patriot spy 😎 )
